name: Water Grey
lede: Water Grey, despite the name, is a dull olive-tan, not a grey, and one of the more frequent matches in our entire painting archive.

sections.title: A grey that isn't grey
sections.body: Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates Water Grey to 1705, plate 14, chip B1 [1]. The ISCC-NBS revision of 1955 files the same chip as "light olive gray," block 91, not as a true grey despite the name [1]. The nearest named neighbor by measured color is [[ecru-olive]], a close match, with [[dull-citrine]] just behind it [2]. Further out, [[dust]] and [[buffy-citrine]] sit in the same small cluster [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a match for Water Grey in 2,216 of 23,781 paintings, about 9.3 percent, more common than 92 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in the 1700s, in 232 of 3,449 paintings, 1.3 times the rate expected from that century's share of the archive [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light tone, in 45 percent of its appearances [3]. Arnoud van Halen used it most: it appears in 28 of his 50 paintings here, 6.4 times his peers' rate [3]. It shares canvases more than chance would predict with colors we call Yellow Stone and Dark Citrine [3]. The earliest archive match dates to 1201, five centuries before Maerz and Paul recorded the name in 1930 [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[3].
